 Autism-therapy workers say big chains pressured them to boost treatment hoursC
 Anna Wilde Mathews , Christopher Weaver , Tom McGinty , The Wall Street Journal 14 min read 21 Oct 2026, 06:47 AM IST 
 Summary
 Medicaid data show some private-equity-backed chains billed far more hours than rivals. Companies say patient needs guide treatment. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Minutes after an autistic 3-year-old lay her head on a Squishmallow stuffed toy and closed her eyes, Abigayle Hosking was ordered to take the makeshift pillow away and rouse the sleepy girl. The child was scheduled for four more hours of autism therapy at the Centria Healthcare clinic in Michigan where Hosking worked until last year.
 Hosking said she felt terrible. “The younger kids, you know, I think they need a break,” she said.
 Medicaid plans and private insurers will often pay for up to about 40 hours of autism therapy a week, and shut-eye doesn’t count. At Centria and some other large chains backed by private-equity investors, former employees said in interviews that they felt pressure to maximize therapy hours, claims the companies dispute.
 The Wall Street Journal analyzed the billings of five of the largest private equity-backed providers of autism therapy to Medicaid patients, including Centria. Together, the group’s average weekly therapy hours for those patients were 29% higher than competitors’ in 2024. All but one of those companies delivered more hours than local rivals.
 “It’s simple business math,” said Philip Painter, a physician who briefly served as chief medical officer at Centria. “You want to maximize the number of hours the child is doing.”
 Medicaid programs financed by state and federal taxpayers paid $10 billion for autism therapy last year, up from around $2 billion in 2021, driven in part by increasing numbers of treatment hours per patient.
 In autism therapy, treatment hours are supposed to be tailored to each patient’s needs, but there is debate about how much is warranted.
 Many autism-therapy providers and an industry group cite studies of young children showing high-hour therapy can help those with severe challenges. Government officials and insurers have scrutinized long hours, at times pointing to other research, disputed by some providers, that raised questions about the correlation between long therapy hours and improved outcomes. New federal guidelines for Medicaid say there is no correlation.
 Private-equity firms have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into building national chains of clinics to serve children diagnosed with autism. The Journal’s autism-treatment analysis looked at Centria, majority-owned by THL Partners; Action Behavior Centers, backed by Charlesbank Capital Partners; Hopebridge, acquired by Arsenal Capital Partners; Cerberus Capital Management-backed Lighthouse Autism Center; and Learn Behavioral, majority-owned by Gryphon Investors, which billed fewer hours a week, on average, than its competitors.
 All five companies said they individualize treatment, including weekly hours, based on patient needs, not financial considerations.
 The four companies with higher-than-average hours said the Journal’s analysis of Medicaid claims didn’t account for differences in the severity of patients’ autism, and that their nap policies aim to accommodate children’s sleep needs. Centria, Action and Lighthouse said their patients had more severe autism than average, justifying more therapy.
 Centria said waking a 3-year-old as described by Hosking wouldn’t have complied with its policies, and such an incident wasn’t documented at the time. Action disputed the assertion in the Medicaid guidelines that treatment intensity doesn’t correlate with outcomes.
 Former employees of the four higher-hour companies said in interviews they felt pressure to recommend long therapy schedules for children, and that centers sometimes turned away children who needed low weekly hours.
 The former employees said the companies applied the same approach to both Medicaid and privately insured patients.
 In Arizona, Centria billed 94% more hours a week per patient, on average, than competitors in 2024, and in Colorado, Action billed 81% more than local rivals, the Medicaid data show.
 LaDeana Thompkins’s son was scheduled for about 40 hours a week at an Action facility near Phoenix when she told the clinic in July that his hours would need to be cut by about half because he was starting kindergarten, according to emails reviewed by the Journal.
 In a meeting the next day, an Action staffer told Thompkins and her husband that their son wasn’t ready for kindergarten, and proposed that the boy, then 5, could delay going to school and continue full-time therapy, according to Thompkins and her husband, as well as documents from the time.
 The couple decided they didn’t want to hold off on kindergarten, where their son could get help from an aide and other support at their local school. The Action staffer told the couple that the clinic could accommodate the boy only if he was attending close to its recommended therapy hours, and that if he left and wanted to return, he might land on a waiting list, the Thompkinses said. “It felt like we just fell off a cliff,” LaDeana Thompkins said.
 Action’s chief clinical officer, Charna Mintz, said in an interview that if a family chooses school, “even if it is not what is clinically recommended,” the company would support the family in the transition. In a letter, lawyers for Action told the Journal the company had “information that would thoroughly debunk the narrative this patient is being used to support,” but couldn’t share it due to a healthcare privacy law.
 The big therapy chains focus on applied behavior analysis, or ABA, commonly given in clinics or at home to children as young as 2. Sessions can include practicing chores such as folding l

docs.title: Safety net cue: India may need to recraft public welfare for the age of artificial intelligence
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Safety net cue: India may need to recraft public welfare for the age of artificial intelligence
 Mint Editorial Board 3 min read 22 Oct 2026, 07:30 AM IST 
 Summary
 The idea of a UBI may need a long-horizon relook in the context of how AI could plausibly reshape India’s economy. As for similar ideas of public welfare, are America’s Big AI companies like Anthropic and SpaceX onto something? 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The idea that every citizen should be awarded an income by the state is not any more ‘radical’ than assuring people basic welfare. That label would apply better to declarations by leaders of artificial intelligence (AI). 
 This week, Elon Musk declared an intent to give “every kid in America” a single share in SpaceX next year. His AI-plus-space business was beaten to the mic by Anthropic, an AI company that committed 5% of its shares to a “public benefit fund” designed to solve problems caused by this technology. 
 One pressing problem may turn out to be a bulk takeover of office jobs by AI. It was once a matter of enlightened self-interest for private industry to help stem discontent with the outcomes of capitalism. 
 Today, that role is best played by Big AI, whose leaders may have figured that awarding people a stake in AI’s rise could co-opt their support. Arguably, this is a longer-horizon bet than the do-gooder image these handouts project, and what grants it strategic value is the universality of the grant’s coverage. 
 Governments must not just take note, but explore how their safety nets could be recrafted for the age of AI. 
 The general concept of a universal basic income (UBI), with the state sending everyone monthly transfers, found advocacy well before the rise of AI. Back then, the pivotal point made against it rested on its ‘moral hazard’: that it would induce laziness. 
 But this, in itself, was a lazy argument. The link between employment and the will and ability of people to work is not hard-set. It can and does snap. The textbook response is a Keynesian stimulus, all forms of which are meant to be brief. 
 While AI is job generative in its own right, as most new technologies are, the human roles it replaces could spell an enduring snap-off that finally dispels the myth of only slackers being jobless in a growing economy. 
 In India’s case, a ‘backward bending labour supply curve’ was once posited as a burden: low-paid workers opt for leisure over work the moment they reckon they have enough money. Rising aspirations have clearly left that worry behind. 
 Yet, its behavioural cues seem to haunt the moral case for a UBI. What India has, instead, is a rash of cash transfer schemes in various states for women who meet specific criteria. Chhattisgarh’s scheme, for example, is aimed at women aged above 21 who are married or once were. 
 The Centre’s constraint is fiscal. Even a modest monthly transfer of ₹ 1,000 to all Indians above 18 but below the income-tax-paying level would cost the exchequer above ₹ 11 trillion annually. This tempts the idea of paying just the half who are under the median level of income. 
 An arbitrary cut-off, however, might not just distort what folks report, it would entail eligibility filters, bureaucratize how we identify the needy and make a ‘type 2 error’ of leaving out multitudes more likely. In other words, India’s economy must expand vastly before we can afford a proper UBI policy. 
 Yet, it might already be time to take a leaf out of Big AI’s playbook. Since India’s digital stack allows cash disbursals, it could conceivably be used to award citizens tiny portfolios of equity in a mix of state-owned enterprises and state-aided startups. 
 If we nudge awardees to hold these shares for future dividends instead of selling them—for which a soft lock-in may work—and these companies do well over time, we’d have a buffer in case the economy tilts further in favour of capital over labour. All in all, it pays to plan long-horizon. Let’s keep our options open.

docs.title: Retirement planning: How much should you invest in stocks and mutual funds after 60? Here's what expert suggests
docs.text:
For someone retiring at 60, the challenge is not simply earning higher returns. It is ensuring that the retirement corpus lasts another 20 to 30 years, even as inflation pushes up household expenses and markets go through periods of volatility. So, how much of a retirement portfolio should remain invested in stocks and equity mutual funds ? According to M. Pattabiraman, founder of personal finance platform Freefincal and professor at IIT Madras, a typical retiree should consider limiting equity exposure to 30% of the retirement corpus. Those with substantially larger savings than required may have greater flexibility to take equity risks. In a Freefincal report, Pattabiraman outlined three principles for determining equity allocation after retirement, focusing on corpus size, inflation-adjusted returns and the ability to withstand prolonged market downturns. During their working years, investors may hold 50-70% of their portfolios in equities to benefit from long-term market growth. However, Pattabiraman argues that this allocation needs to be reconsidered once regular withdrawals begin. His framework suggests keeping equity exposure below 30% for a typical retirement, although the appropriate allocation depends on the size of the corpus and the investor's financial circumstances. For instance, consider two retirees who each need ₹ 6 lakh annually to meet expenses. One has accumulated ₹ 1.8 crore, equivalent to 30 times annual expenses, while the other has ₹ 4.5 crore, or 75 times annual expenses. The second retiree has a much larger financial cushion and may be better positioned to withstand equity market volatility. These are illustrative examples, not specific portfolio recommendations. Freefincal's retirement planning tool also suggests different equity allocations depending on the retirement age. Even someone retiring at 30 has an illustrative equity allocation of just 37%. Early retirement means a longer period of withdrawals and greater exposure to multiple market cycles. Pattabiraman also cautions against assuming that retirement investments will consistently generate returns above inflation. He recommends planning with a post-tax real return of no more than zero, or even a negative real return of 1-2% for a more conservative estimate. For example, if inflation averages 6%, a zero real-return assumption means investment returns merely keep pace with rising living costs. Another concern is sequence-of-returns risk. If markets fall sharply during the initial years of retirement, investors withdrawing money for household expenses may be forced to sell equity investments at depressed prices. Even if markets subsequently recover, the withdrawals made during the downturn could permanently weaken the portfolio. This is why Pattabiraman's approach prioritises controlling equity exposure rather than depending on higher market returns to fund retirement. Pattabiraman's third principle involves building sufficient fixed-income resources to support inflation-adjusted expenses during the first 15 years of retirement. If this is achievable, retirees can consider a bucket strategy, separating money needed for regular expenses from investments intended for longer-term growth. Under this approach, a 20-30% equity allocation could potentially remain untouched for several years, reducing the need to sell stocks or mutual funds during market downturns. He also suggests considering pension plans or multiple annuity income streams alongside the bucket strategy to strengthen retirement income security. However, retirees must account for inflation because fixed-income products do not necessarily provide income that rises with living costs. The broader takeaway from Pattabiraman's analysis is that retirement portfolios should be designed around the sustainability of withdrawals rather than maximising investment returns. For someone approaching retirement, the decision on equity exposure should therefore depend on the retirement corpus, expected expenses, available fixed-income resources and ability to withstand market volatility. Kirti Jha is a Senior Content Producer at Mint, where she writes on mutual funds, taxation, personal finance and macroeconomic developments. Her reporting focuses on helping readers understand complex financial developments through data-driven, research-backed stories that explain how policy changes, market trends and regulatory decisions affect investors and households.

Before joining Mint, Kirti worked at ET Money, where she specialised in mutual fund research and investment analysis. She tracked portfolio disclosures, fund manager strategies, sectoral allocation shifts and investment trends, distilling large datasets into investor-focused insights. Her work combined quantitative analysis with consumer-centric storytelling, enabling readers to better understand fund positioning, portfolio changes and long-term investment opportunities.

Kirti holds a Bachelor's degree in Economics from Indraprastha College for Women, University of Delhi, and a Master's in Finance from the Jindal School of Banking & Finance at O.P. Jindal Global University. Her academic training emphasised analytical thinking, quantitative research and financial decision-making, providing a strong foundation in understanding capital markets, financial systems and economic policy. With a combined experience in investment research and financial journalism, she is committed to producing accurate, accessible and insightful journalism that empowers readers to make well-informed financial decisions. docs.title: SIR issue: We must separate allegations and questions of legality from the hardships caused to citizens
docs.text:
Opinion 
 SIR issue: We must separate allegations and questions of legality from the hardships caused to citizens
 Jagvir Singh 5 min read 21 Oct 2026, 02:00 PM IST 
 Summary
 Both clean rolls and inclusive franchise are indispensable—they are not competing democratic values. When it comes to the legitimacy of the process, neither an allegation of conspiracy nor an assertion of administrative good faith can substitute evidence to settle the matter. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls has become an extraordinary political conflagration. An Indian Express report’s claim that some decisions were taken despite two election commissioners repeatedly dissenting to them gave the opposition munition to allege that the SIR exercise presided over by the chief election commissioner (CEC) has led to large scale disenfranchisement engineered to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). 
 Amid this cacophony, three distinct questions deserve dispassionate independent examination: One , is the SIR lawful? Two , were the Commission’s decisions lawfully made? And three , did deletions materially alter electoral outcomes? Conflating them produces more heat than illumination. 
 Electoral rolls are not immutable registers. Article 324 of the Constitution entrusts their supervision to the Election Commission. Sections 21 and 22 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 provide for their revision and correction, including special revision under Section 21 (3). 
 The objective is as elementary as to retain every eligible elector while removing entries of the deceased, duplicates and persons no longer ordinarily resident in a constituency. After decades of migration, urbanization and imperfect record-keeping, periodic intensive verification is not only permissible, but maintaining accurate rolls is a statutory responsibility of the Commission. 
 In Association for Democratic Reforms v. Election Commission of India & Anr ., decided on 27 May 2026, the Supreme Court sustained the Commission’s power to undertake SIR, including across multiple constituencies. That disposes of the broad objection that an intensive revision is inherently unconstitutional. It does not, however, immunize every administrative direction, altered form or individual deletion from judicial scrutiny. The distinction is fundamental. 
 The apparently startling figure of about 13.39 crore names classified during SIR has been explained by the Commission as ‘ASDD’, or absent, shifted, dead and duplicate—9.5 crore as absent and permanently shifted; 2.7 crore as deceased; and 1.01 crore as duplicate. These are the entries identified principally at the draft-roll stage and should not be equated with 13.39 crore eligible voters being disenfranchised. 
 In an electorate as vast and mobile as India’s, deaths, migration and change of residence inevitably leave electoral rolls carrying substantial obsolete or duplicate entries. Identifying such entries is the raison d’être of an intensive revision. 
 The exercise also does not end with their initial identification. Claims, objections and restorations precede preparation of the final rolls, providing an opportunity to eligible electors inadvertently left out to be restored. 
 The second controversy concerns institutional decision-making. Indian Express reports at least 14 recorded objections by commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, particularly to an SIR-linked declaration inserted in the online Form 6. The Commission maintains that its ultimate decisions were unanimous. 
 Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 requires unanimity for regulating business procedure and allocation, and envisages unanimity where possible, or majority decision on other matters. 
 Moreover, a statutory registration form cannot casually be rewritten through a software interface. The Supreme Court has expressly clarified that it has neither approved nor disapproved the modified Form 6 and, on 14 October, stated that it might pronounce an order to take care of the concern on 28 October. 
 Who authorized what and pursuant to which lawful process are questions for the court to determine. Demands for the resignation of the CEC before that determination substitute political verdict for judicial inquiry. 
 Third, did the deletions engineer electoral victories? This is an empirical proposition, not one established by repeating the aggregate number. Thousands of booth-level officers, drawn from different backgrounds and political persuasions, participated. 
 A centrally designed, geographically selective manipulation across this dispersed workforce would require coordination, incentives or concealed controls that ought to leave detectable traces. Its complexity makes the allegation demanding to prove, if not impossible. 
 Constituency-level evidence offers a useful check. Hindustan Times (9 October), citing Election Commission data, reported that the five West Bengal seats with most names removed from the 28 February roll were all won by the All India Trinamool Congress; the five with the fewest deletions by BJP. This pattern rebuts any simple inference of a BJP victory from deletion volume. 
 There is, however, one criticism that scarcely needs forensic sophistication. The exercise has imposed considerable inconvenience on ordinary citizens. 
 Antiquated spelling and address records, relocation, inconsistent legacy-roll linkages, unfamiliar digital procedures and unevenly motivated and trained ground personnel have made verification needlessly onerous. India’s familiar weakness of sound policy undermined by haphazard execution has again manifested itself. 
 Remedies are eminently practicable.

 Industry body flags unintended consequences of CCPA’s proposed ad guidelines for small businesses
 Nabodita Ganguly 5 min read 21 Oct 2026, 11:33 AM IST 
 Summary
 India SME Forum has urged the government to reconsider parts of the CCPA's proposed anti-spam advertising rules, arguing that compliance requirements could burden small businesses that lack dedicated compliance teams. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 New Delhi: The small-business lobby, India SME Forum, has said that the government's proposed crackdown on spam marketing could increase compliance costs for thousands of micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs). 
 The forum, which represents nearly 100,000 small businesses, has asked the consumer affairs ministry to assess the impact of the proposed rules before rolling them out. Requirements such as managing customer consent, maintaining records and handling complaints could be especially challenging for smaller firms that do not have separate compliance teams, it said. Mint has seen a copy of the representation sent to the consumer affairs ministry on 15 October. 
 The issue has arisen as digital advertising has become a key channel for growth and customer acquisition for businesses. Digital advertising revenue jumped 26% to ₹ 94,700 crore in 2025, according to a Ficci-EY report, making up nearly two-thirds of India's overall advertising market.
 Consumer groups, however, have welcomed the draft framework. They argue that stricter consent requirements, disclosure of AI-generated communications and greater accountability for outsourced marketing activity could help reduce spam calls that continue to frustrate consumers. 
 The proposed Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Pesky, Promotional and Unsolicited Commercial Communications, 2026, aim to protect consumers from unfair trade practices and violations of their rights arising from unwanted promotional and marketing communications. The draft guidelines will come into force only after their final publication by the Central Consumer Protection Authority ( CCPA ).
 The forum, which represents businesses such as J B Chemicals & Pharmaceuticals, a pharmaceutical manufacturer; Emmbi Industries, a polymer-based packaging company; and Varun Agro Food Processing, argues that small businesses are often run by a single person who handles sales, customer service and administrative work, frequently using the same phone number for all these activities. 
 Until press time, the ministry did not respond to Mint’s queries. 
 Consent requirements key industry concern
 The CCPA draft requires businesses to obtain consumers' consent before sending brand promotions and to wait 45-90 days before reaching out again if they opt out.
 However, the forum said the requirement for product-specific consent needs clarification, especially for retailers and service providers offering multiple products. It further suggested allowing consent for clearly defined product or service categories, subject to consumer choice and purpose limitations.
 The forum also called for simple, accessible cons ent methods for non-telecom channels, including customer replies, website forms, and QR code subscriptions.
 Meanwhile, industry experts argue that the guidelines could lead to a sharp increase in calls seeking consent for advertisements, making it difficult for businesses to reach consumers. 
 “We've done a study in 2024, where we surveyed 300 businesses, and almost 90% or more said that it is imperative for revenue generation and customer acquisition, not only domestically, but across borders as well,” said Meghna Bal, director of the Esya Centre, a tech-policy-focused think tank. Removing this channel could make it harder for consumers to find new products, she said. 
 UK introduced its Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations in 2003, bringing them into force on 11 December that year. The European Union adopted its ePrivacy Directive in July 2002, while US introduced its Telemarketing Sales Rule in 1995 and established the National Do Not Call Registry in 2003. These frameworks regulate unsolicited marketing through requirements governing consent, disclosures and opt-outs. 
 The US experience demonstrates that regulatory curbs can reduce spam calls over time. Despite a rise in complaints in FY2025, unwanted-call complaints remained about 48% lower than FY2021 levels after the introduction of measures such as the National Do Not Call Registry and stricter telemarketing rules. 
 The proposed guidelines state that businesses must clearly disclose at the start of a communication if they use AI-generated voices or text on behalf of a brand. Without this disclosure, the communication may be treated as unsolicited or unwarranted. 
 The India SME Forum urged regulators to distinguish between fully automated communications and human-reviewed messages using AI tools , while setting clear disclosure requirements for automated interactions.
 Backing for stricter accountability steps 
 Meanwhile, some argue that the draft, if implemented, will help consumers. 
 Online citizen-engagement platform and pollster LocalCircles' latest survey found that 97% of mobile users still receive spam calls daily, many of them from 10-digit numbers that fall outside existing telecom rules. Founder Sachin Taparia welcomed CCPA's move to hold brands accountable for calls made directly or through outsourced agents. 
 "We are confident that once callers have to verify their identity, disclose AI-generated calls upfront and resolve complaints within 7 days, consumers will be able to tell a genuine call from a fraud, and we will see significantly fewer pesky and misleading calls across telecom and digital platforms. For legitimate businesses, small or large, compliance is simple—take consent, identify yourself and honour the opt-out," Taparia said. 
 Key Takeaways
 MSMEs

Opinion 
 Building India’s deep-tech enterprise pipeline: from IP to IPO
 Padmaja Ruparel 12 min read 21 Oct 2026, 08:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 Capital is only one component of enterprise creation. Entrepreneurs need mentors versed in science and markets, industry partners to test technology, specialised labs, help with regulatory approvals and standards, and tech-transfer offices that protect intellectual property (IP). 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 As entrepreneurial energy plays an ever-larger role in India’s success story, we present a package of weekly opinion articles by members of TiE, a global organization for startups and entrepreneurs. From the rural reach of India’s startup revolution and the easing of capital and compliance challenges to the role of angel investors, how startups and micro, small, and medium enterprises must grow together and how best to track innovation, TiE authors cover a wide spectrum of relevant issues. 
 ***
 India’s startup ecosystem is entering a more challenging phase. The focus is shifting from counting startups, patents or funding rounds to evaluating how many Indian technologies move from lab validation to global markets and become established, publicly accountable enterprises.
 Beyond the startup count
 India has demonstrated significant progress in fostering startups. As of March, the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) had recognized as many as 223,000 startups. Over 13,000 new patent applications were filed by startups, but many were abandoned and only 2,174 were granted. The moot point is that once filed, is the patent for technology differentiation really followed up to create a product for commercialization? Most of these intellectual properties (IPs) are viewed as a “protection” rather than “assets”. And that’s moot in today’s fast-evolving, technology-led world.
 Today, nearly 92% of the market capitalization of the S&P 500 is derived from intangible assets—brands, IP, software and data—up from just 17% in 1975. Global spending on intangible investment has crossed $4.7 trillion a year in advanced economies, overtaking investment in physical infrastructure. This is one of the most significant shifts in modern economic history: the countries that lead are no longer those with the largest industrial base, but those that own the world’s most valuable IP and brands. India’s next chapter will therefore be defined not by “Make in India,” but by the ambition to own the world.
 India’s real gap is the gap from research to IP, then to products, companies and global scale. Deeptech startups build on scientific breakthroughs in fields like materials, semiconductors, biotech, space, robotics, energy and quantum computing—domains where the IP is not adjacent to the business; it is the business itself. Therefore, the better measure of success is whether a startup becomes a professionally managed enterprise that outlasts its founders.
 Deeptech changes the equation
 This dynamic creates a fundamentally different development trajectory. Deeptech companies may require several years to transition from laboratory research to commercial scale and face numerous risks. Scientific concepts may not prove viable, and technologies that succeed in laboratory settings can fail in practical applications. Securing regulatory approvals and certifications often requires several years, and customer adoption of new technologies may be slow. These firms typically require multiple funding rounds before generating substantial revenue, thereby increasing capital risk.
 Applying expectations of rapid revenue growth, as seen in software companies, can result in premature down-rounds, underinvestment or the abandonment of strategically significant technologies. The implication is evident: deeptech sectors demand not only patient capital but also enduring institutional support, testing facilities, early customers and constant strategic guidance.
 What global firms reveal
 The most instructive global examples extend beyond narratives of venture funding. They show that deeptech companies are built through coordinated systems spanning research, infrastructure, customer engagement, manufacturing partnerships, long-term technical roadmaps, building talent and, of course, funding.
 IBM aims to deliver a large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029 and is pursuing interim demonstrations of quantum advantage. The lesson: breakthrough technologies attract investment when progress is shown as clear, measurable technical milestones, not vague promises of future disruption.
 Emerging artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure firms are commercializing via distribution partnerships. For example, Fundamental raised funding while securing deployment through Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure and customer channels. For Indian deeptech firms, the central question extends beyond funding. It is critical to understand the need for institutions that can facilitate the achievement of technical, industrial and commercial milestones, and the ways through which they can do so.
 The bridge is more than money
 Over two decades of India’s startup journey, one lesson is clear: capital is only one component of enterprise creation. Entrepreneurs need mentors versed in science and markets, industry partners to test technology, specialized labs, help with regulatory approvals and standards, and tech-transfer offices that protect IP, forge industrial ties, support spin-outs and negotiate founder-friendly licences—plus early-adopter customers and investors.
 India needs to move beyond a narrow focus on patent counts. A patent may be legally valid yet commercially insignificant. For deeptech firms, the most valuable IP often extends beyond the patent itself—to proprietary algorithms, industrial designs, scientific datasets, differentiated know-how and trusted brands. Wi

docs.title: Devina Mehra: Inefficient markets and what they mean for investors
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Devina Mehra: Inefficient markets and what they mean for investors
 Devina Mehra 4 min read 21 Oct 2026, 12:21 PM IST 
 Summary
 For long, the efficient market theory was the prevailing wisdom being taught in universities. But closer inspection reveals why this idea doesn't hold in real life. And who better to guide investors and regulators on how markets can go wrong than George Soros? 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 As I write this on Vijayadashmi day, I remember the legend that even as Ravana lay dying, Lord Rama asked his brother Lakshmana to sit at his feet as a disciple and get knowledge. In the same spirit, I am sharing insights from George Soros’ long record as a successful trader and investor—the very person many in India love to hate. 
 In fact , whenever anyone has asked me whether even after recognizing a bubble one can play it and get out in time, my answer has been that the only person who has managed to do that more than once at scale is Soros. Others are one-trick ponies who may have been permanently bearish or bullish and got lucky that one time. 
 Soros’ basic insight was that unlike what has been the conventional wisdom, markets are not efficient. When I came into markets over three decades ago, the efficient market theory was the prevailing wisdom being taught in every university—that all available information is already there in asset prices, markets tend to move towards equilibrium and that deviations occur in a random fashion and can be attributed to extraneous shocks. 
 It was clear to me right away that this did not hold in real life. Think about it: if the price of a stock moves from ₹ 100 to ₹ 150 in a quarter when no new information has come, which of the two prices is the efficient one? 
 A beloved offshoot of this theory is the calculation of ‘ beta ,’ which measures how much a stock moves when the market moves by a certain percentage. Again, if you calculate this for each stock, you will find that the beta changes all the time and can hardly be used to predict anything. Soros’ insight went a step further to say that not only are markets inefficient, they are inefficient in certain predictable ways. 
 His framework rests on two cardinal principles. One , market prices distort underlying fundamentals, ranging from negligible to significant deviations. Two , reflexivity, which means that not only do fundamentals determine market prices, but through feedback loops, especially via leverage like debt and equity, the underlying fundamentals can be altered. 
 Sometimes this is simple. For example, in a cyclical industry like cement or steel, when the cycle turns up, the worst company gives you the biggest stock market pop because a small operating margin improvement becomes a big change in its net profit and hence share price. Then the company usually raises capital at the higher stock price, reducing debt and making its financials look even better. The stock price reflexively changes the fundamentals. 
 This is a relatively benign example, but when this happens at scale across a market, it can cause a bubble. 
 ​According to Soros, every market bubble comprises an underlying real-world trend and a prevailing misconception that reinforce each other. They progress through four distinct stages. 
 The inception is when an underlying trend and a misconception turn mutually reinforcing. In most bubbles, there is an underlying trend to start with. Then this mutual reinforcement accelerates if the bubble survives initial negative feedback tests. 
 In a real estate bubble, for instance, the misconception can be that not only are property prices rising, there is no problem with credit because the loans are secured against real estate. This does not recognize the fact that property prices are themselves largely dependent on the easy availability of credit. So, it becomes a self-reinforcing loop. 
 Also, leverage does not only mean excess debt in the system. It can also be over investment and over valuation on the equity side. The latter is largely what happened during the internet boom. Before that, in the 1960s, the US had a conglomerate boom, with companies acquiring others to artificially boost earnings per share, fuelled by inflated stock prices until reality collapsed expectations. 
 Currently, this is most evident in the artificial intelligence (AI) space, where equity valuations have long lost touch with reality and an estimated $1 trillion of credit has also gone in to fund AI. Anthropic, a leader in the field, is borrowing in dollars at over 10%. 
 After the acceleration in the boom comes the twilight period, when expectations diverge wildly from reality and doubts grow, but the momentum persists out of inertia; and when CEOs are telling themselves “to keep dancing until the music stops,” as was said during the mortgage boom before the global financial crisis of 2008-09. This is a suspended animation sort of period. 
 Finally, reality catches up, triggering a sharp bust. Prices typically go even below fair value due to forced liquidations and financial panic. The pendulum swings the other way. 
 During the global financial crisis, the BSE Sensex fell from a peak of 21,206 in January 2008 to 8,160 in March 2009—A decline of about 61%. The fact that markets are neither self-regulating nor in equilibrium makes a case for regulatory intervention. Regulators must actively work to prevent bubbles from growing too large, rather than assume that markets are always right. 
 Indeed, financial crises typically become the impetus for regulatory reform. For example, the US Securities and Exchange Commission came into being as a result of the Great Depression. 
 The author is founder of First Global and author of ‘Money, Myths and Mantras: The Ultimate Investment Guide’. Her X handle is @devinamehra

 Trump promises cash and bailouts to woo midterm voters worried about high prices
 Marianne LeVine , Natalie Andrews , The Wall Street Journal 6 min read 21 Oct 2026, 06:44 AM IST 
 Summary
 The president has laid out plans for an $8 billion bailout for farmers as voters raise concerns about costs. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 $5,000 for every American adult. An $8 billion bailout for farmers. $90 payments for seniors.
 President Trump is relying on a new strategy to salvage Republican seats in the midterm elections: promising an array of financial benefits to Americans, some of which he said he would only deliver if his party defies the polls and keeps control of Congress.
 The president started his campaign to put cash in the pockets of voters during Republicans’ midterm convention in September, when he announced a $1 trillion proposal to send $5,000 to each adult citizen—if the GOP holds on to its congressional majority. Since then, Trump has sent $90 to Medicare recipients to offset premiums and $500 checks to nearly one million people for what the administration called excessive fees under the Affordable Care Act.
 On Monday, Trump said he would send $8 billion in direct payments to U.S. farmers, some of whom have soured on the president amid his tariffs and as prices for diesel, gasoline and fertilizer have risen since his war with Iran. And on Tuesday, the president announced a new program that would provide up to $30,000 to Americans if they report a tip about government fraud.
 The White House is also discussing rolling out executive orders in the remaining days before the midterms aimed at addressing high prices, including one focused on reducing housing costs, according to people familiar with the matter.
 Republicans are facing one of the toughest midterm environments of any party in years, and the series of policy announcements serve as both an effort to motivate voters and a tacit acknowledgment that people are hurting financially. Democrats have accused the president of trying to buy votes.
 Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, described Trump as the “unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party,” and said that “the choice has never been clearer: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, common-sense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction.”
 The pledges get cheers at rallies where Trump supporters don red hats and wait in long lines to get a prime spot, but it is unclear if they will turn out the voters that Republicans need, those who vote conservative but tend to stay home during elections when Trump isn’t on the ballot.
 A Wall Street Journal poll last month found that voters aren’t sold on Trump’s proposed $5,000 checks, with 64% of respondents calling it a bad idea.
 Trump outlined the $8 billion farm bailout during a rally Monday in Kansas, telling his supporters that the Agriculture Department would launch a “Harvest Fuel Relief program” that would help offset rising diesel costs as farmers harvest their crops.
 “And when the Republicans win, we will pass even more funding for our farmers,” Trump said at the rally.
 Trump also said he would sign legislation permitting the year-round sale of gasoline blended with 15% ethanol, a long-sought-after policy by U.S. corn growers. Congress has to first pass the legislation, which faces an uphill climb. Trump said he would only agree to the policy if Republican Sen. Roger Marshall wins in Kansas against Democratic opponent Adam Hamilton.
 “With Roger Marshall in the Senate, we will make year-round E-15 permanent,” Trump said. “But if Adam Hamilton is in, I’m not doing it.”
 The president has also made several announcements about new projects that are intended to benefit states that will help determine which party controls Congress. The president last week wrote on social media that Taiwan had committed to buy natural gas from a proposed export terminal in Alaska. ​​And he highlighted a Minnesota company’s plan to build a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa.
 During a House Finance Committee hearing in September, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent answered questions about President Trump’s plan to pay each adult citizen $5,000 if Republicans win the midterm elections. Photo: Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg News
 Some of the benefits have already been distributed to voters. The $500 Affordable Care Act refund checks went out on Oct. 1 (alongside a letter touting his record on cutting healthcare costs), and the $90 payments to Medicare recipients were deposited in bank accounts or sent out on Oct. 8.
 But the president’s proposal to dole out $5,000 checks to Americans, which Trump has said would be contingent on the GOP keeping control of Congress, is expected to face hurdles. Democrats and some Republicans have expressed skepticism, raising concerns that such a move would balloon budget deficits and fuel inflation. Sending $5,000 to every American adult would likely cost well over $1 trillion, the Journal has previously reported.
 The federal government has made direct payments to Americans in the past. In the 2020 election, as Trump was running for re-election and the Covid pandemic ravaged the country, the government sent out $1,200 checks to tens of millions of Americans that arrived signed by Trump with letters from the White House taking credit for a bipartisan deal passed by Congress.
 In 2022, then-President Joe Biden said he would forgive up to $20,000 in federal student loan debt for tens of millions of Americans. Conservatives dismissed the move as an attempt to win over young voters ahead of that year’s midterm elections. Democrats lost nine seats in the House and gained one seat in the Senate.
 Democrats say Trump’s proposals won’t move the needle in this year’s midterms, where concerns about affordability are top of mind for voters.

docs.title: French protests: Why is one of the rich world's biggest spenders on public services burning?
docs.text:
Opinion 
 French protests: Why is one of the rich world's biggest spenders on public services burning?
 Lionel Laurent 4 min read 21 Oct 2026, 03:07 PM IST 
 Summary
 The country's propensity to descend into unrest has become scarily regular. The discontent that provided the kindling for the fiery protests was already there—government after government has prioritized pensions over the future of young people. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Anyone walking along the boulevards of Paris on Sunday afternoon will have sensed the “shame and anger” described by President Emmanuel Macron after a weekend of rioting. 
 It’s not only France that’s feeling the heat. Anger about rising inflation, from energy prices to housing costs, has led to clashes in Italy and Portugal. It may also lose President Donald Trump the US midterm elections given the impact of his folly in the Strait of Hormuz on oil prices. 
 Still, France’s propensity to descend into unrest has become scarily regular, as has the inability of Macron’s administration to get a grip. Which begs the question: Why is one of the rich world’s biggest public spenders on fire again? This is after all a highly redistributive country that has racked up an extra €1 trillion ($1.1 trillion) of borrowing since 2019. 
 And yet surveys indicate that the French on average lack €500 a month to comfortably cover their outgoings, making them vulnerable to sudden changes in their economic situation—and likelier to protest. 
 On one level, the sparks that lit the flames this time around included multiple short-term political failures that echo the Yellow Vest riots of 2018. The authorities clearly weren’t expecting more than half a million people to take to the streets nationwide, let alone the thousands of looters in Marseille. 
 The mayor of Limoges, whose town hall was broken into and gutted by fire, has called for more resources for a police force he described as outgunned by far-left opportunists. And the government’s inability to engage with or defuse earlier protests by high schoolers—driven by a lack of fiscal headroom to throw money at the problem as bond yields, and hence state borrowing costs, rise—fuelled the fire. 
 But the discontent that provided the kindling was already there. And one big reason is that French public spending is allocated in a very lopsided way. 
 Compare the France of 2024 with that of 1974—the last year it balanced the budget—and there’s been very little change in spending on public services such as security, the courts or education as a percentage of GDP. 
 The biggest beneficiaries, as usual in the West, are pensioners. Spending on them has jumped by 6.5 [percentage] points, with successive governments prioritizing a generous retirement over the future of young people entering education and the workforce. Almost a third of France’s education budget goes on pensions, for example, which may explain why teachers’ wages are below the OECD average. 
 Alongside the frustrations of underpaid public servants are signs that adding more jobs in the private sector—the focus of Macron’s labour-market reforms—increasingly doesn’t pay. That €500 monthly gap in people’s monthly outgoings is hard to fill via the career ladder as lower productivity, declining education standards and an innovation lag drag wages down while ever-higher social charges eat into take-home pay. 
 Statistics agency INSEE has estimated that an employer raising a minimum-wage worker’s salary by about €440 would result in a take-home gain of only €100. Le Monde estimates that the French median wage has risen 22.8% since 2017, outpaced by inflation of 23.4%. 
 This doesn’t excuse the weekend’s violence. French purchasing power is slowing down, not reversing. Yet the combination of grievance politics, intergenerational unfairness and an inescapable sense of decline is what makes France feel fragile despite its size and its still considerable strengths. It also makes compromise harder, with the new Yellow Vests bemoaning low wages and high taxes over the weekend alongside nihilistic masked mobs spray-painting “ACAB.” 
 With Macron a spent force, the question is the 2027 presidential election. The sight of cities on fire will doubtless create new supporters for far-right leader Marine Le Pen. Her extreme-left opponent Jean-Luc Melenchon is being seen as the instigator of the mayhem on the streets. In a vote dominated by cost-of-living and security fears, the far right holds several cards—including the Trumpian promise of putting hundreds of euros into people’s pockets by cutting payments to the European Union. 
 Still, six months is an age in politics. Le Pen’s plans involve billions in new spending and lack credibility, according to Bloomberg Economics. Voters are slowly starting to understand that rising state debt is a problem. Meanwhile, centre-left politician Raphael Glucksmann, who has ruled out an alliance with Melenchon, is enjoying a poll surge of his own. 
 But what’s missing in this crowded race, as elsewhere in Europe, is honesty on the reforms needed—both from politicians and the ageing electorates that are blocking inescapable change. ©Bloomberg 
 The author is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist writing about the future of money and the future of Europe.

docs.title: Germany’s young conservatives are angry with their own party
docs.text:
Global 
 Germany’s young conservatives are angry with their own party
 The Economist 4 min read 21 Oct 2026, 06:31 PM IST 
 Summary
 The JU is where Germany’s ambitious conservatives come to network, drink and complain about the Mutterpartei (mother party, ie, the CDU). They are a lively bunch, if not a diverse one: bar a smattering of women, almost everyone seems to be called Johannes. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 SUCH IS THE power of the Junge Union (JU), the youth branch of Germany’s ruling centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), that all the party’s big beasts feel obliged to pay it homage. At last weekend’s JU congress in Bonn, each was given a prizefighter’s entrance, complete with flashing spotlights and theme music selected by the organisers.
 Friedrich Merz, the CDU’s embattled chancellor, will have been happy with “We stay united through the storm”. Hendrik Wüst, the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia and a potential challenger to Mr Merz, looked a little bewildered on entering to the thump of “You should know that baby you’re the best”, before delivering a dull speech. As for the congress’s slogan, “Tomorrow is loading”, it seemed either an ironic nod to information-superhighway dreams of yore or an attempt to sound vaguely digital. Either way, it was better than the toe-curling Denglish of last year’s “What the Future?!”
 The JU is where Germany’s ambitious conservatives come to network, drink and complain about the Mutterpartei (mother party, ie, the CDU). They are a lively bunch, if not a diverse one: bar a smattering of women, almost everyone seems to be called Johannes. The most important is the 34-year-old Johannes Winkel, head of the JU, who has emerged as an irritant for Mr Merz. Last year Mr Winkel threatened to torpedo the government’s plan to raise pensions. In his speech this year he said the CDU was living in the past, passing off minor tweaks as ambitious “reforms” and risking extinction. The JU’s opinions matter because their group in the Bundestag has 20 MPs—which, as members point out, is larger than the 12-seat majority held by Mr Merz’s coalition. Mr Winkel has warned that last year’s insurrection will pale next to what will come if a new pension reform, designed to rein in costs, is watered down.
 If these young conservatives are angry, it is because nothing hurts so much as betrayal. It was the true believers of the JU who formed the vanguard of Mr Merz’s multiple attempts to become CDU leader, the third of which succeeded in 2021. At last, they thought, a true-blooded conservative saviour to wash away the mushy centrism of the long Angela Merkel years. (One thing the JU and Mr Merz agree on is that Mrs Merkel’s 16-year reign was an embarrassment.)
 But since Mr Merz won last year’s election it has been disappointment upon disappointment: borrowing binges, in-fighting and endless concessions to the Social Democrats (SPD), the junior coalition partner. At last year’s youth bash Mr Merz alienated everyone by urging the JU to cool its reformist zeal. This year he was on best behaviour, offering full support for the proposed pension reform. His speech “wasn’t a success, but it wasn’t a failure”, sniffed one delegate.
 Mr Merz also showed he can press the crowd’s buttons. He earned the weekend’s biggest applause by deploring a proposed coalition in Berlin led by the populist-left Die Linke party, which won a recent election in the capital. Many in the CDU, and beyond, believe that party’s Berlin branch is crawling with antisemites and subversives. Yet just as the delegates’ fury peaked, Die Linke clinched an agreement with the Greens and SPD to begin coalition talks. That inspired the JU to pass a resolution, spearheaded by another Johannes, demanding “political and social ostracism” of any such government. It featured a picture of a young man in a keffiyeh and the slogan Nie wieder ist jetzt! (“Never again is now!”), a rather hysterical invocation of the Holocaust.
 These days it is easier for youth delegates to rage against leftists than against the populist-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). The CDU as a whole has not gone soft on the party that has destroyed its polling lead; Mr Merz had harsh words for the AfD, too. But some CDU delegates in the parliament of Saxony-Anhalt, an eastern state where the AfD won a near-majority in an election last month, may soon break the party line and give the radicals the votes they need to take office there. The CDU in Saxony-Anhalt, sighs a third Johannes, is an “unguided missile”.
 No wonder delegates struggled to believe that the CDU had figured out how to recover. “The party is crumbling,” confided one, adding that he is embarrassed to tell his friends he is a member. The CDU’s young guard seems to be bursting with self-confidence at precisely the moment it has lost faith in the Mutterpartei. But as one CDU grandee puts it, the JU always thrives when its elders are struggling. Kids tend to think they know best. And these ones have the numbers in parliament to prove it.

docs.title: How to measure returns on AI
docs.text:
Global 
 How to measure returns on AI
 The Economist 4 min read 21 Oct 2026, 06:31 PM IST 
 Summary
 From tokenmaxxing to something more normal 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 In the beginning there was AI, and bosses everywhere lost their minds and said you must all use this technology no matter whether it is useful and no matter how much it costs. And they introduced AI leaderboards and came up with stupid words like “tokenmaxxing”. And lo, usage did indeed rise. And then the bosses remembered some very basic concepts like “budgets” and realised that this might not be such a great idea after all. And then a different question rang through the boardrooms, and this question was about returns, and it was harder to answer.
 This potted Genesis of AI adoption is not entirely fair. As long as organisations are trying to encourage usage, it can still make sense to look at things like employees’ token consumption. “I would expect software engineers to spend more money than a finance analyst,” says the boss of one software firm. “But anyone within finance, it shouldn’t be zero.”
 But usage (also known as input) measures don’t tell you whether any value is being created. And even when AI is producing benefits, points out Mika Ruokonen of LUT University in Finland, lots of them accrue quietly to individuals in the form of scattered time savings. If an extra hour or two of an employee’s time has been freed up to shop on Vinted, someone has benefited (mainly Vinted) but it isn’t your company (unless you work at Vinted).
 Shifting the focus to returns on AI investment means concentrating more on outcomes-based measures, such as team productivity or customer satisfaction. But these require careful thought. Scientists, for example, are using AI to produce more papers (yay!) of dubious merit (boo!). A recent study by Tulsi Suchak of the University of Surrey and her co-authors found that papers derived from a health and nutrition data set ticked along at an average of four a year between 2014 and 2021; in the first nine months of 2024, there were 190.
 So outcomes-based measures have to be designed to capture both positive and negative effects of AI. At Google, for example, engineers have long been measured on three dimensions. Speed is one: how long does a code review take, say. Ease is another: how much friction is there in the system for things like onboarding new developers. The last, critically, is quality: “I don’t want to just go fast and make it easy to ship terrible software,” says Richard Seroter of Google Cloud.
 Complicating matters further is the fact that it often takes a while for the benefits of AI to show up. People have to spend time learning how to use the technology. Increased output can create bottlenecks elsewhere. A paper published last year by Kristina McElheran of the University of Toronto and her co-authors looked at AI adoption among American manufacturing firms, and confirmed the existence of a “J-curve” in which productivity dips before it leads to an improvement. This effect is especially pronounced at established firms and seems to be partly explained by changes to management practices that had previously helped firms to keep tabs on performance. Any kind of calculation about projected returns has to take this initial period of disruption into account.
 Bosses also have to take a view on something much more fundamental: what kind of return are they interested in? One way to show financial returns on AI is to seize on time savings as an excuse to cut headcount. For some jobs and in some circumstances, that might make sense. But chainsaws and employee morale go together about as well as salt and slugs. And people who are no longer there cannot be redeployed in more productive ways. A better option is to calculate the amount of money that AI saves on expanding headcount. (Working out how much extra revenue can be attributed to the technology is even more of an art; at the very least, you need good baseline data and a culture of A/B testing to isolate its effects.)
 On top of everything, there is wild uncertainty about where AI is heading. That is an argument for a third set of measures, to go alongside ones on inputs and outcomes. These measures, which Mr Seroter calls “organisation-based”, are more geared towards capturing how well change is being managed. They could include data on levels of employee satisfaction with the way AI has been implemented, or progress towards building in-house expertise in areas that AI will not automate. A one-eyed focus on usage ignores the importance of returns. A rigid focus on returns ignores the need to keep learning.

docs.text:
Long Story 
 Beyond the great smog: A year-round silt crisis choking urban India
 Sayantan Bera 9 min read 21 Oct 2026, 05:00 PM IST 
 Summary
 Winter smog makes headlines, but toxic road silt never settles. With dust loads in Indian urban areas up to 30 times above many global cities, the country’s clean air fight faces an invisible wall. A ground report from the dustbowl of Gurugram. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Gurugram: Every morning, Sumit Tayal, 38, a resident of Ballabgarh in Haryana, takes a state roadways bus to reach Sadar Bazar, the old shopping district in Gurugram. Tayal has been working at a garment store in the market for more than a decade. Over the years, as traffic on the roads multiplied, it took Tayal more and more time to cover the 45-km distance between Ballabgarh and Gurugram. These days, it takes him about two and a half hours each way, or five hours of commute—daily.
 Tayal makes this journey every day of the week, including on weekends. But the most distressing part of the ride is the air he is forced to breathe and the unmeasured quantities of dust he inhales.
 “The roads are very dusty and trucks carrying construction material and debris without a cover add to the problem,” Tayal said.
 As a consequence, he often suffers from coughing bouts and respiratory tract infections, which intensify during the winter months when air pollution levels spike.
 Tayal is a fervent advocate of public transport and joined Clean Air Bharat, a citizen activist group with chapters in multiple cities. “Because I post on (civic) issues like illegal waste burning and unpaved or dug up roads, my social media account is blocked repeatedly,” Tayal said.
 Nirvana Country, in another part of Gurugram in Sector 50, is a world away from the chaos of Sadar Bazar. It is a gated residential society comprising independent houses, with a planned layout and lush greenery. It appears to be an ocean of calm compared to the din and dust that engulfs it—a debris hill on the edge and roads laden with dust. A conversation with a resident here bridges the miles separating Nirvana from Sadar Bazar.
 Anup Sood, who moved into Nirvana in 2007, says it’s been a downhill journey when it comes to quality of life. Sood’s son was born in 2010 and the child was diagnosed with allergic rhinitis (inflammation of nasal passages as a reaction to airborne allergens) when he was just five, following exposure to dust and dirty air. His son, now 16, is unable to take part in physically demanding sports like football. The winters are a tough time for the family as the kid often suffers from wheezing and needs frequent nebulization.
 “We are seriously contemplating moving out of Gurugram to a place where the air is breathable,” Sood said.
 Ruchika Sethi, who founded Clean Air Bharat in 2016, also a resident of Nirvana, minces no words while describing the situation in the city: “Living here reminds me of the iconic (1979) film Kala Patthar and the mine workers covered in soot. In the Gurugram of 2026, the black soot is replaced by a grey-white film of dust.”
 The sources of dust, Sethi says, are local and very controllable. Most of it comes from dumping of construction and demolition waste in open areas, following little or no dust management protocols during construction, and unpaved and dug up roads.
 “In Mumbai, they have the Malabar Hills (an upscale residential area) but what we have here are ‘malba’ hills,” she said.
 Malba is Hindi for construction debris. Sethi has seen countless such hills gain height over the years, including one which abuts her home in Nirvana Country.
 Gurugram’s rapid transformation from a quiet backcountry to a rapidly urbanizing corporate hub at the turn of the century earned it the moniker ‘millennium city’. In reality, it scorches in summer, floods during monsoon, and turns into a gas chamber during winter. The dust, however, is always around, like a shroud hanging over the metropolis.
 Air pollution in the Delhi-National Capital Region is no longer a problem limited to winter months , said Arunesh Kumar, a pulmonologist. “Prolonged exposure is leading to COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) and asthma. We are increasingly seeing such cases among non-smokers. Similarly, I am seeing cases of lung cancer among young patients who are non-smokers and have no family history of cancer,” he said.
 Lives lost
 Yet, Gurugram is not an exception. Many Indian cities have literally turned into dustbowls. Silt loads on Indian roads are 25-30 times more than in developed countries, found a 2024 paper by researchers from the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Delhi and Kanpur (published in the journal Science of the Total Environment).
 The researchers, who collected data from 259 locations in 32 cities across India, found that road dust levels exceeded World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines in 55% of cases. They estimated that about 10,000 lives are lost annually due to PM2.5 pollution attributable to road dust.
 The State of the Global Air Report 2025, put together by the Boston-based Health Effects Institute and the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, located at the University of Washington School of Medicine, attributes more than two million deaths in India to air pollution.
 PM2.5 refers to particulate matter less than 2.5 microns in size while PM10 are larger particles with a diameter of less than 10 microns; both are harmful pollutants that are easily inhalable due to their tiny size. The IIT study also noted that road dust emissions contribute 30-60% of PM2.5 and PM10 levels in metropolitan regions in India.
 A 2026 working paper by WRI India, an environment think tank, found that silt load values in three cities—Mumbai, Ahmedabad and Indore—varied between one and 20 gram/square meter (a measure of the weight of dust over a specific area). The highest silt loa

docs.title: Nvidia’s $10 billion AI data center quick-fix and the winning stocks
docs.text:

 Nvidia’s $10 billion AI data center quick-fix and the winning stocks
 Jack Denton , Barrons 1 min read 21 Oct 2026, 06:23 PM IST 
 Summary
 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang unveiled plans for modular, quickly-deployed data centers to begin AI work while permanent infrastructure is being built. These component stocks could be winners. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s opening-salvo pitch in the chip giant leader’s keynote speech at GTC Berlin is modular, quickly-deployed data centers that would dramatically reduce the time until AI computing can take place. There are also key stocks set to benefit too.
 “This will change the way people install and build data centers,” Huang said, pitching Nvidia’s new Vera Rubin DSX Pods.
 “An AI factory can take several months to build. Until it is operational, it produces no tokens,” Huang said, referring to the basic units of data processed by AI models. “We are announcing DSX Pod, bringing [our] full-stack platform into a factory-built, integrated system.”
 “DSX Pods are integrated, fully-cabled and factory tested, then delivered in transportable containers,” said Huang. “Once site utilities are ready, estimated deployment goes from several months to days.”
 It’s a data center quick-fix that could not only save billions of dollars—but also benefit component stocks.
 AI data centers can take months of assembly, with any delays being extremely costly.
 “If we said it’s $40 billion per year of revenue generation that comes out of that infrastructure … if delayed by just three months that’s $10 billion worth of revenue, [which] would make anyone anxious,” Huang said.
 The DSX Pods would essentially allow data centers under construction to begin operating using the shipping container-like modules, before eventually being hooked up to permanent infrastructure. It could bring data center construction from four to five months down to a month, Nvidia’s CEO said.
 Nvidia disclosed some of its partners involved in components for the DSX Pods—stocks that, if the concept takes off, could be major winners.
 Those partners include PC and server makers, namely Dell Technologies, Lenovo, and HPE, as well as contract manufacturers like Wistron. “Neoclouds,” such as Singapore’s DayOne—which has expressed an intent to go public via American Depositary Shares (ADSs) on the Nasdaq—would also be included, as well as nuts-and-bolts power players like Schneider Electric.
 Nvidia stock was 1.5% higher in premarket trading on Wednesday as Huang continued to speak.
 Dell stock was up 4.9%, with HPE up 3.6%. Lenovo shares traded 2.9% higher in Hong Kong before Huang’s keynote, with Wistron advancing 3.2% in Taipei by the Asian close. Schneider Electric was hovering around flat in French trading.

 Small influencers make a big festive splash this season
 Rudrani Chattopadhyay 5 min read 22 Oct 2026, 06:01 AM IST 
 Summary
 Smaller social media influencers are enjoying a bumper festive season this year, with some earning up to five times more from brand deals. As brands turn to smaller, regional creators to reach local shoppers, higher campaign fees are boosting paydays even as consumer spending remains under pressure. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 India's smaller media influencers are enjoying a bumper festive season, with some doubling or even quintupling their earnings from brand collaborations this season. More deals and higher campaign fees are driving the windfall, as brands are turning to smaller, regional and vernacular creators to woo shoppers through familiar cultural connections, even as inflation squeezes household budgets and threatens to dampen festive spending. 
 “The festive season is a peak period for consumer spending, making it important for brands to reach shoppers when they are more likely to make purchases,” said Tarun Bansal, founder of influencer marketing and talent management agency Viral Fuel Studios. 
 Brands are now looking beyond reach to engagement, consumer trust and purchase intent, Bansal said. “Regional creators and vernacular content can help brands connect with consumers in tier-2 and tier-3 markets, where local languages and cultural references can shape how audiences respond to products,” he added. 
 Beauty, fashion and lifestyle creator Pallabi Paul Kundu, co-founder of AmPal Ads, an influencer marketing agency, said brands are favouring nano creators—who have 1,000-10,000 followers each—for mass campaigns involving 100-200 creators or more, often within budgets similar to those of the previous year. Last year, brands worked with 10-20 macro creators—who have over 100,000 followers each—as well as micro creators with 10,000-100,000 followers. 
 Kundu’s own festive season campaign fees rose around 20%, as her Instagram following grew from 55,000 to 60,000 between 2025 and 2026. 
 More deals, higher fees 
 For some creators, higher earnings came with more brand deals. 
 Lifestyle creator from Delhi, Gaurika Gandhi, who has 140,000 Instagram followers, completed 45 paid collaborations this festive season, an 18.4% rise from 38 last year. Her earnings for the period rose nearly 60% from a year ago. 
 Kolkata-based lifestyle creator Kritika Pareek, who has 11,100 Instagram followers, reported that her festive season earnings grew nearly fivefold over a year, while her average fee per campaign increased 40%. And b eauty and fashion creator Anuska Sinha (@junscameraroll) with 22,000 Instagram followers, reported a nearly 100% increase in earnings this season. “Last year, I did more barter collaborations, whereas this year, since I have moved away from barter, I received a lot more paid collaboration opportunities,” said Sinha, who works out of Kolkata and Mumbai. In a barter collaboration, a brand gives creators a product or service in exchange for promotional content, rather than a fee. 
 Other creators earned more without any increase in the number of collaborations. Naveen Yadav, who works from Haryana and Germany, runs the movie, OTT and music promotions page Flicks and Funnys, completed five paid collaborations during this festive season, the same number as in 2025. But his earnings for the season doubled from around ₹ 50,000 to ₹ 1 lakh, thanks to the rise in his fees. “Most of our brand deals this festive season came from movie promotion agencies, music labels and event companies,” said Yadav. 
 And some creators reported higher earnings even as their number of paid collaborations fell, with higher payouts helping offset the decline in deal volumes. Lifestyle creator Dipshikha Biswas, with her @trickswithdips handle, who has 95,100 followers, did two paid collaborations this season, as against four in 2025. “My earnings doubled from ₹ 30,000 to ₹ 60,000,” she said. 
 Beauty and lifestyle creator Soumasree Ghosh, @beautificsoumi, who has 87,500 followers, saw her paid collaborations fall from five last year to two this season. However, her earnings rose 20%, from ₹ 25,000 to ₹ 30,000 . 
 Late campaign planning and shorter delivery timelines emerged as concerns for creators and agencies. Kundu said one of the main issues for Kolkata-based AmPal Ads was that campaign planning began later than usual. “Durga Puja campaigns started around the first week of September this year, compared with the last week of July in 2025. Brands often expected creators to deliver content within 24-48 hours, leaving little time for planning, scripting and shooting,” she said. 
 Viral Fuel's Bansal said that as brands moved away from celebrity creators towards a wider mix of regional, micro and nano creators to drive local engagement, sourcing and vetting multiple creators across languages and regional markets added to the campaign planning time. “Final strategies often got bogged down in discussions around the regional mix and language nuances, pushing back the rollout of briefs,” he said. 
 Pareek said enquiries were higher than last year, but only a few resulted in paid collaborations. Of her four Durga Puja deals, two came after the festival had already begun. Some brands expected content on the same day the brief was shared or within the next two days. 
 Brands bet on local connections
 Beauty brands accounted for the higher-value collaborations, according to Kundu, while food brands generated more deals but contributed less revenue, with most collaborations relying on barter arrangements. 
 Cross-brand collaborations also featured in this year’s Durga Puja marketing. Pareek cited a campaign by quick-commerce platform Zepto and cosmetics brand Blue Heaven. The brands did not respond to Mint ’s queries until press time.
